stem:
A 7-year-old girl fell onto her outstretched left hand from the monkey bars. She is tender over the distal forearm with no deformity, and her hand is neurovascularly intact. The X-ray shows a bulge in the dorsal cortex of the distal radial metaphysis, with the volar cortex intact, no angulation and a normal physis.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Above-elbow casting for 6 weeks is for unstable forearm fractures. A buckle fracture is stable and heals in about 3 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: Closed reduction under sedation, then cast
options.explanation: Reduction is for angulation beyond age limits, such as more than 15 degrees at 5-10 years. This fracture has no angulation.

options.label: C
options.text: Below-elbow cast and X-ray review at 1 week
options.explanation: Casting with a fracture-clinic X-ray is for complete or greenstick metaphyseal fractures. Buckle fractures need no follow-up film or review.

options.label: D
options.text: Removable splint for 3 weeks, no follow-up
options.explanation: A buckle fracture is stable: a removable wrist splint or backslab for comfort for 3 weeks, taken off at home, with no clinic review or repeat X-ray.

options.label: E
options.text: Collar and cuff sling for 3 weeks
options.explanation: A sling does not immobilise the wrist and will not control pain from a distal radius fracture.

context: Distal radius buckle fractures are stable: a removable splint for 3 weeks, removed at home, with no repeat X-ray or fracture-clinic review.
